The Scaly rockcod Trematomus loennbergii, a nototheniid endemic to the high-latitude Southern Ocean, exhibits a life history finely tuned to persistent near-freezing conditions. Field surveys of adult specimens from McMurdo Sound indicate that individuals can attain a maximum total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that places this species among the medium-bodied nototheniids. The onset of gonadal development, marking sexual maturation, occurs at a considerably smaller size; histological examination of ovarian tissue in collected fish reveals that puberty is initiated at a total length of 19.1 centimeters [Lp = 19.1 centimeters]. This pattern suggests a prolonged juvenile phase dedicated to somatic growth before reproductive investment commences. The body mass associated with these size thresholds has been estimated from length-weight regressions derived from local sampling campaigns. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, emerging from demersal eggs with an average diameter of 1.8 millimeters, possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0031 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0031 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva. In contrast, adults approaching their asymptotic length exhibit a substantially greater body mass, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at 270 grams [Wwi = 270 grams] for the largest individuals, illustrating the considerable mass gain achieved over the course of the lifespan.

Reproductive output in Trematomus loennbergii has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions designed to mimic the stable thermal environment of the nearshore Antarctic benthos. At a constant water temperature of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C], gravid females that had been acclimated to this regime were observed to release their ova during a single protracted spawning event. Analysis of batch fecundity from these trials demonstrated that an individual female produces approximately 36 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 36 eggs per spawning event], with a single such event occurring annually [F_R_i = single such event occurring annually]. This annual reproductive cycle, whereby a female releases all of her vitellogenic oocytes in one synchronized batch per year, is consistent with the pattern seen in several other high-latitude nototheniids. The extended interval between spawning events, coupled with the modest clutch size, suggests a conservative reproductive strategy that prioritizes the production of large, yolk-rich eggs capable of sustaining the embryo through a lengthy incubation period at subzero temperatures. The energetic investment per offspring appears substantial when compared to temperate teleosts of similar body size.

Embryonic development and the early life stages of Scaly rockcod are critically dependent on thermal conditions, given the extreme cold of their natural habitat. Investigations on the closely related species Trematomus bernacchii have provided a useful comparative basis for estimating hatching schedules in T. loennbergii. Based on these analogies, the age at birth, defined as the interval between egg fertilisation and chorion rupture, is expected to be approximately 66 days [ab = approximately 66 days] when incubation proceeds at a stable temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. This protracted embryogenesis is characteristic of Antarctic notothenioids and reflects the profound deceleration of metabolic and enzymatic processes at low temperatures. The newly emerged larva, still reliant on its endogenous yolk reserves, must navigate a brief pelagic phase before settling to the benthos. The transition from the lecithotrophic larval stage to exogenous feeding marks a critical bottleneck in the early life history, as the timing of first prey capture must coincide with the availability of suitable microzooplankton. The slow pace of early development, measured in weeks rather than days, underscores the challenges of completing the larval period in a persistently cold environment.

The trajectory from juvenile to adult in Trematomus loennbergii is characterized by a gradual accumulation of body mass and the eventual attainment of reproductive competence. Length-based estimates derived from field-collected specimens indicate that the wet weight at puberty, the mass at which an individual first exhibits mature gonadal tissue, is approximately 62.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 62.2 grams]. This represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass, reflecting the accumulation of somatic tissue and energy reserves necessary to support the metabolic demands of gametogenesis. The corresponding length at puberty of 19.1 centimeters [Lp = 19.1 centimeters] marks a clear threshold in the species life history, beyond which resources are directed toward both continued somatic growth and reproductive effort. The disparity between the wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0031 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0031 grams] and the wet weight at puberty of 62.2 grams [Wwp = 62.2 grams] illustrates a roughly four-order-of-magnitude increase in body mass during the juvenile phase, a growth trajectory that is relatively slow compared to temperate notothenioids. This protracted period of somatic development is likely a consequence of the low metabolic rates and reduced feeding opportunities at subzero temperatures.

Lifespan and maximum age in Trematomus loennbergii have been inferred from otolith increment analysis and size-frequency distributions of populations sampled from the Ross Sea. The maximum recorded longevity, based on the oldest individuals encountered in these surveys, is approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years] for fish that have completed their life cycle under the ambient thermal regime of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C]. This extended lifespan is typical of Antarctic nototheniids, which generally exhibit slow growth, deferred maturity, and exceptional longevity relative to temperate teleosts. The age at death corresponding to this lifespan underscores the species' extremely slow pace of life, a syndrome that also encompasses the protracted embryonic development of 66 days [ab = 66 days] at 0 °C [T = 0 °C] and the relatively modest annual reproductive output of 36 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 36 eggs per spawning event] occurring once per year [F_R_i = once per year]. Terminal body dimensions documented in this species include a total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] and a body mass of 270 grams [Wwi = 270 grams], reflecting the maximum size attained after decades of growth in the frigid Ross Sea habitat.
